title: was never written down by the man it's named after.
description:
was never written down by the man it's named after. Dwight Eisenhower said it out loud in a single 1954 speech. He never called it a method, a matrix, or a rule.

Told an audience at Northwestern University that he had two kinds of problems, the urgent and the important, and that the urgent are never important while the important are never urgent.

He said he was quoting a former college president. The actual transcript names no one. Northwestern's real president was sitting in the same room and was praised separately in the same speech, which is likely why his name gets wrongly attached to the quote online.

Turned Eisenhower's spoken line into a drawn two-by-two grid in his book The 7 Habits of Highly Effective People, sorting tasks into urgent, important, both or neither, and telling readers to live in the important-but-not-urgent quadrant.

Copies of Covey's book sold by the time he died in 2012, the book that turned a single unattributed line from a 1954 speech into a permanent planning grid.

The Eisenhower Matrix is named after a man who borrowed the words, popularised by a man who drew the grid thirty-five years later.

Sources:
- https://www.presidency.ucsb.edu/documents/address-the-second-assembly-the-world-council-churches-evanston-illinois - read in full 7 Sep 2026: The American Presidency Project, full transcript of Dwight Eisenhower's address at Northwestern University, 19 August 1954. Establishes the exact wording, that Eisenhower said he had two kinds of problems, the urgent and the important, that the urgent are not important and the important are never urgent, and that he introduced the line explicitly as the statement of a former college president, rather than claiming it as his own words, while Northwestern's actual president, Dr J. Roscoe Miller, was seated in the audience and praised separately in the same passage.
- https://quoteinvestigator.com/2014/05/09/urgent/ - read in full 7 Sep 2026: Quote Investigator. Confirms the 1954 Eisenhower speech is the earliest known instance of the saying, that Eisenhower attributed it to an unnamed former college president rather than to himself or to Miller, and traces later published versions from 1954 onward that add the word seldom and increasingly credit the line to Eisenhower directly rather than to his unnamed source.
- https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_7_Habits_of_Highly_Effective_People - read in full 7 Sep 2026: Wikipedia. Confirms the book was first published in 1989 by Stephen R. Covey, that Habit 3 lays out four quadrants sorted by urgent versus important with the advice to prioritise quadrant two, not urgent but important, and that the book had sold more than 20 million copies by the time Covey died in 2012.
